exp.0:1:
He says that God speaks with force, like a roaring lion, from Zion, that is, from Jerusalem. When his voice is heard, the pastures and fields of the shepherds are filled with mourning, and the top of Carmel, a mountain known for its greenness, dries up.

Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa, in Judah, and God sent him to speak to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. This verse opens his book as a warning: the God of Jerusalem is going to judge. The texts that follow show that he begins with the neighboring nations and then reaches Israel, because of its injustices.

Today, this verse reminds us that the voice of God is not an ornament. If he speaks to us through his Word, it is wise to listen with humility and to correct what he points out to us, before hardening our hearts.
exp.0:3:
It says that God will send fire as punishment upon the house of Hazael, and that this fire will destroy the fortresses or palaces of Ben-hadad. "I will send fire" means that God will bring destruction, and the phrase about devouring means that it will consume everything completely. Hazael and Ben-hadad were kings of Syria, whose capital was Damascus.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who announces judgment against the nations neighboring Israel. Damascus had treated Gilead with great cruelty, and the text compares this to threshing with iron sledges. God does not overlook violence against peoples. Scholars debate which specific events the names of the kings refer to, but the general message is clear.

For today: God sees injustice, even when the powerful seem untouchable. This invites us to treat the weak with compassion and to trust that God will bring justice in his time.
exp.0:6:
God says he will send fire on the wall of Gaza, and that fire will destroy its palaces, that is, the strong houses of its rulers. It is a way of saying that the city, with all its power and pride, will be brought down.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. He is judging the nations neighboring Israel. Gaza was a city of the Philistines, and it is accused of having taken whole peoples captive to hand them over to Edom, probably as slaves. God does not overlook that cruelty. Many scholars think the fire is an image of God's judgment, although we do not know in detail how it was fulfilled.

For today: God sees how we treat people, especially the most vulnerable. We can ask ourselves whether we take advantage of others in any way, and ask him to make us just and compassionate.
exp.0:7:
The explanation says that God will destroy the people of Ashdod and the rulers of Ashkelon. He will also raise his hand against Ekron, and what is left of the Philistines will perish. "Cut off" means to destroy completely, to cut down to the root; "turn my hand" means to act again with his power; "remnant" means those who survive. Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron were Philistine cities, together with Gaza.

God speaks through the prophet Amos and announces judgment on the nations neighboring Israel. Gaza had taken whole peoples captive to hand them over as slaves to Edom. Here the judgment extends to the other Philistine cities. Some think all of them shared that guilt, although the text does not spell this out.

For today: God sees cruelty against others, even when no one punishes it. We can ask ourselves whether in some way we treat others as if they did not matter, and ask him to make us just and compassionate.
exp.0:11:
It says that God will send fire on Teman and Bosra, two important cities of Edom. The fire represents destruction through war, and the palaces stand for the power and security of the people. Teman and Bosra are mentioned as examples of all of Edom.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a relative of Israel, but it attacked Israel with violence and held a grudge for a long time. For this reason God announces judgment. The text does not say exactly when or how this happened; many read it as a warning of later invasions.

For today: a grudge kept for years is a serious sin before God, even when no one sees it. If there is someone you are holding anger against, ask God to help you forgive and to seek peace, instead of feeding bitterness.
exp.1:4:
God says that he will send fire upon Judah, and that this fire will destroy the palaces of Jerusalem. The fire is a common image in the prophets for war and invasion that sweeps away everything in its path.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Amos, who announced judgment on several nations. Here it is Judah's turn, the people of God, because they despised his law, did not keep his commandments, and let themselves be deceived by lies, as their ancestors had. The palaces represent the pride and the sense of security they had. Many understand this as a announcement of the fall of Jerusalem, which happened centuries later.

For today: it is not enough to know God; we must obey him. Examine which lies lead you to live without taking his Word seriously, and return to it with humility.
exp.1:6:
They say some want to see the poor brought down low, as if they wished for dust on their heads. They turn aside the way of the humble, that is, they shut them out from justice. Father and son go in to the same young woman, which seems to point to sexual abuse or immorality that dishonors God. By this they profane his holy name.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, addressed to the kingdom of Israel. God accuses his people of injustice: they sell the needy, take advantage of the weak, and mix their religious life with abuse. For this reason he announces punishment. Scholars debate the exact detail of the young woman, but all of them see an accusation of abuse.

For today: God watches how we treat the weak. Today I can examine how I treat those who depend on me, such as employees, family members, or poor neighbors, and defend their justice and dignity with concrete actions.
exp.1:7:
It says that some in Israel would lie down to rest on clothes they had taken as security for a debt, beside the altars. They also drank wine bought with fines or penalties collected from others, and they did this in the temple of their gods. The first word refers to those who had been fined, and the second means taken as a pledge for a loan.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, in the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses his people of injustice toward the poor. The law required that a cloak taken as a pledge be returned at sunset (Exodus 22:26-27), because the poor person needed it to keep warm. Here religion is mixed with abuse.

For today: we cannot separate worship from justice. Let us examine whether, at work, in business, or in our daily dealings, we take advantage of someone weak, and seek to treat everyone with honesty and compassion.
exp.1:12:
God says that He Himself will press Israel down in their own place, like a cart loaded with sheaves (bundles of cut wheat) that creaks and strains under the weight. The phrase is hard to translate. Some understand that God will crush the people; others, that God will make the ground groan beneath them the way the cart groans under its load.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. He has just recalled that he raised up prophets and Nazirites (people set apart for God) among them, yet the people made the Nazirites drink wine, which their vow forbade, and ordered the prophets to be silent. It is a judgment for rejecting the voice of God.

For today: when God speaks to us through His Word, let us not silence it or push it aside because it makes us uncomfortable. Listening in time and obeying with humility spares us from heavier burdens.
exp.1:14:
It says that when God's judgment comes, no one will be able to save themselves through their own abilities. The archer will not stand firm, the swift runner will not manage to escape, and the horseman on his horse will not save his life either.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who announced his message to the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier, God had reminded them how much he had cared for them, but they oppressed the poor and despised his word. For this reason he warns them that not even the strongest or swiftest soldiers will be able to escape the consequences.

For today: do not place your trust in your strength, your intelligence, your money, or your experience. All of that is limited. Live with humility before God, listen to his correction, and seek his mercy, because only he can truly sustain us.
exp.2:3:
This verse asks two questions whose answer is obvious: a lion does not roar in the forest if it has no prey, and a young lion does not growl in its den if it has caught nothing. The roar shows that something has already happened.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to Israel. He comes after a series of questions that show every effect has a cause. God has just said that Israel is his chosen people and that for this reason he will correct them for their wickedness. Amos makes clear that his message is not his own idea: God has spoken, and so he must prophesy.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is not by chance. Let us take his warnings seriously, and respond with humility and obedience before the consequences arrive.
exp.2:4:
This verse asks two questions whose answer is obvious. A bird does not fall into a trap if no one has set it, and the trap does not spring up from the ground if it has caught nothing. Everything has a cause.

The prophet Amos is speaking to the people of Israel. Using everyday examples, such as two people who walk together or the lion that roars, he shows that things do not happen by chance. He wants them to understand that the warnings and judgments he announces have a cause: God is speaking, and they must listen.

For today: when we face difficulties or warnings, it is good to stop and ask what God may be telling us, instead of assuming that everything is coincidence. Let us ask for humility to hear his voice in the Bible and to change course in time.
exp.2:7:
This verse asks two questions whose answer is obvious. If a lion roars nearby, everyone trembles with fear. In the same way, if God speaks, the prophet cannot stay silent.

The prophet Amos speaks to the people of Israel, the northern kingdom, in a time of prosperity, but also of injustice and oppression. Before this, he gives examples of cause and effect: a trumpet alarms the people, and nothing happens without a cause. Likewise, Amos says that his message is not his own idea; God spoke to him, and so he must warn the people.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is not to be ignored. We can ask him for the courage to obey him first, and to share with love and truth what he has shown us.
exp.2:8:
God commands that a message be announced from the palaces of Ashdod, a Philistine city, and from those of Egypt. He invites them to gather on the mountains of Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, to see what is happening there. The message is proclaimed aloud. What they will see are the great tumults (abuse of the weak and injustice and wickedness) in the midst of the city.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who addresses Israel. The neighboring peoples, known for their harshness, are called as witnesses. The idea is that even they would be astonished at so much injustice among God's people. The following verses say that they were piling up riches through plunder, and that for this judgment would come.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially the weak. Today you can examine whether in your work, your home, or your business you act with justice and honesty, and stand up for those who have no voice.
exp.2:13:
God says that when the day comes to hold Israel accountable for its rebellions, he will also punish the altars at Bethel. The horns of the altar were the projections at its corners, where people would seek refuge and forgiveness. They will be cut off and fall to the ground. Here, the word "visit" means coming to judge.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Amos, who was sent to the northern kingdom. Bethel was a center of worship where the people practiced a religion full of rituals, yet they lived with injustice and oppression. The verses before this one say that only a few would be saved, like the remnants a shepherd rescues from a lion. So neither the temple nor the rituals would protect the people.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we trust our religious customs more than we trust in truly living with justice and repentance. God is not impressed by rituals if the heart remains far from him.
exp.2:14:
He says God will strike both the winter house and the summer house, that is, the residences where the wealthy spent each season. He also says the houses of ivory, meaning mansions decorated with inlays of that material, will perish. Many great houses will be left in ruins.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos to the northern kingdom, Israel. God accuses the people of rebellion, especially the rich who lived in luxury while oppressing the poor. This announcement is part of his judgment. It is commonly understood to refer to the fall of Israel to Assyria, although the text does not give the details.

For today: wealth does not protect us from God. It is wise to examine how we use what we have, and to ask ourselves whether we share it with justice and generosity, rather than trusting in comforts.
exp.3:9:
God says that he sent a deadly plague upon Israel, similar to the one sent upon Egypt. The young men died in war, and even the horses were taken away. The stench of the camps was so strong that it rose up into the nostrils. Yet the people did not return to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel in the north. This verse is part of a series of punishments, such as famine, drought, and plagues, that God used to call his people back to himself. Each time it ends the same way: yet they did not return to him. His aim was not to destroy, but to awaken their hearts.

When difficulties come, we can ask whether God is inviting us to return to him. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but it is always a good time to examine the heart and draw near to him with humility.
exp.3:10:
God says that he sent Israel a destruction so great that it was like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. The people who survived were like a half-burned log snatched from the fire just in time. Even so, the people did not return to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier he had already mentioned famine, plagues, and war. His purpose was not only to punish, but to call the people back to himself. Each warning was an opportunity to repent, and the people let it pass by.

For today: when we go through a crisis or escape a danger, let us not take it as mere chance. Let us ask ourselves humbly whether God is inviting us to return to him, and let us answer him with a sincere heart.
exp.4:11:
God says he knows well the many rebellions and the great sins of his people. He accuses them of mistreating the righteous, of taking bribes, and of keeping the poor from receiving justice at the gate, that is, in the city's court.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel. In that time the city gates were the place where the elders judged cases. The leaders and the rich corrupted that place, hated anyone who corrected them, and grew rich at the expense of the poor. That is why God warns them that they will not enjoy what they have built and planted.

For today: if you have any influence, whether in your work, your church, or your family, use it with honesty. Do not accept unfair advantages, and courageously defend those who have no voice or resources.
exp.4:15:
God, the Lord of hosts, announces a great grief among the people. In the squares and the streets there will be crying and shouts of "Alas! Alas!" Even the farmers will be called to weep, along with those who were skilled at singing laments. A lament is a sad song sung at a funeral, and weeping means crying out in sorrow.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who addresses the kingdom of Israel. Earlier he had asked them to seek good, hate evil, and practice justice at the gate, the place where judgment was made. Since the people did not repent, God warns that a judgment is coming that will reach everyone, and that his day would bring not joy but darkness.

For today: it is not enough to say that God is with us; we must live in line with that. Today you can choose one concrete act of justice or honesty, and ask God for a heart that loves what is good.
exp.4:17:
Woe to you who long for the day of the Lord! What good is it for you? The day of the Lord will be darkness, not light.

This verse says that it is a serious mistake to long for the day of the Lord without being prepared. "Woe" is a word of warning and grief. "Darkness" speaks of judgment and distress, and "light" speaks of salvation and joy. God asks them what they hope to gain, because that day would not be what they expected.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the people of Israel, the northern kingdom. Many expected that day as a victory over their enemies, but they were living in injustice and empty religion. The verses before this one speak of weeping in the streets and in the vineyards, because God would pass through in judgment. Scholars agree that the day of the Lord was the moment when God would act decisively.

Today we can examine our hearts before we ask God to act. It is not enough to say that we belong to him; God expects a life of justice, humility, and sincere obedience.
exp.4:19:
This verse is a question that already carries its own answer: the day of the Lord will be darkness, not light. It is a total darkness, without even a ray of brightness. "Brightness" here means light or radiance, the same word the verse uses. Just before this, Amos says that day would be like fleeing from a lion only to meet a bear, or like coming home, leaning against the wall, and being bitten by a snake.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. Many people expected the "day of the Lord" to be a sure victory over their enemies. But they were living with injustice and empty religion, and God tells them that day would reach them too. For this reason he rejects their festivals and offerings.

For today: it is not enough to sing, attend, or give offerings if we live with injustice. Let us examine our hearts and practice honesty and compassion toward others.
exp.4:20:
God says that he hates and rejects the religious festivals of his people. The sacred festivals are the holy feasts, and the assemblies are the gatherings for worship. "I will not smell in your solemn assemblies" means that he does not take pleasure in them, like a sacrifice whose aroma is not accepted.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, sent to the northern kingdom of Israel. The people performed their rituals with enthusiasm, but they lived with injustice, mistreating the poor. Because of this, the day of the LORD, which they expected as a victory, would be darkness and judgment for them.

For today: God is not satisfied with songs and gatherings if the heart does not obey. Before going to church, ask yourself whether you are treating your family, your coworkers, and those in need with justice and kindness.
exp.4:21:
God says that even though the people bring him burnt offerings (offerings that were burned whole on the altar) and gifts (grain offerings), he will not accept them. The fellowship offerings and the choice animals, the best of the flock, are included in this rejection. He will not even look at them.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel. The people were very religious, with festivals and sacrifices, yet they practiced injustice and oppressed the poor. For this reason God rejects their worship, and right after this he calls for justice and righteousness to flow like a stream that never runs dry.

For today: it is not enough to sing, give, or attend church if we live without justice and compassion. Examine how you treat those who depend on you or have less than you, and let your worship show itself in concrete actions.
exp.4:22:
God tells Israel to take away from him the noise of their songs. He does not want to hear the music of their harps and instruments. Words of praise sung with music are part of this, and the phrase about many songs points to so many of them that they sound like nothing but noise.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, in the northern kingdom of Israel. The people kept their festivals, offerings and songs, but they practiced injustice and oppressed the poor. For this reason God rejects their worship. He does not despise worship in itself, but he rejects it when it is separated from a just life, as the next verse asks.

For today: before you sing on Sunday, review how you have treated others during the week. Ask forgiveness, repair any harm you have done, and help someone in need. In this way your praise will be sincere and pleasing to God.
exp.5:1:
The verse invites the people to travel in their minds to three famous cities: Calneh, great Hamath, and Gath of the Philistines. Then it asks a question: are those kingdoms better than Judah and Israel? Is their territory larger than yours? Some scholars debate how to read the passage: some believe it presumes Israel's advantage, others that it recalls the fall of those cities as a warning.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to Israel in a time of prosperity, when the leaders lived secure and carefree. God confronts them because they trusted in their power and comfort, without seeing their injustice or the judgment that was drawing near.

For today: do not trust in your security, your achievements, or your comfort as if they were an eternal guarantee. Stop to examine whether you are living with humility and justice before God, and do not forget those who suffer around you.
exp.5:5:
They drink wine from large bowls, not from simple cups, and they put on the most expensive perfumes and oils. But they feel no grief over the ruin of Joseph, which here refers to the people of Israel, especially the northern kingdom.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, a shepherd from Judah sent to the northern kingdom. He rebukes the wealthy leaders who lived in luxury and security while the nation was collapsing morally and socially. The following verse announces that they will be the first to go into exile, because their pride and indifference offended God.

Today it invites us to examine whether our comfort has made us insensitive. We can ask God for a compassionate heart and do something concrete: pray, visit, or help someone who is suffering near us.
exp.5:6:
They say that the rich and carefree of Israel, who live among feasts and luxuries, will be the first to be led away captive. The phrase that they will go first means they will lead the line of those taken into exile. The noise of the banquet refers to the revelry where people reclined on their couches to eat. That feast will come to an end.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom. The leaders enjoyed music, wine, and perfumes, yet they felt no grief over the moral and social ruin of their people. God warns them that their comfort will not save them from judgment.

For today: ask yourself whether your comfort has made you indifferent to the suffering of others. Ask God for a sensitive heart, and do one concrete thing this week to help someone who is suffering.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that if ten men were left together in one house, they would all die. It is a stark image: no one would escape.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to Israel, the northern kingdom. The Israelites lived in luxury, injustice and pride, and felt secure. God announces a severe judgment through an enemy, and here shows that not even those who survived a first wave would be spared. Many understand this to refer to war and disease, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with indifference. If we live at ease while ignoring justice and God, it is wise to stop, examine the heart, and return to Him in humility while there is still time.
exp.5:10:
God himself will give the command, and the judgment will come upon everyone. Both the great house, the house of the rich, and the small house, the house of the poor, will be left in ruins. The phrase about striking with cracks means that it will be struck until it is broken into pieces, and the cracks are fissures or splits.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to the kingdom of Israel. Its leaders lived at ease and trusted in their own strength, yet they oppressed others and bent justice. The preceding passage describes a time of death and fear so great that people do not even dare to name God. Some think they fear drawing his attention; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: let us not trust in what we have, whether a house, money, or success. Let us ask God for a heart that loves justice and treats others well, because only what is right with him remains firm.
exp.5:11:
The passage says that what Israel did is as absurd as expecting horses to run over rocks or plowing a rock with oxen. That makes no sense. Yet they turned right judgment (justice, fair dealing) into poison, and the fruit of righteousness into bitter wormwood, a bitter plant. In other words, they made bitter and harmful what was meant to be good.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. They were comfortable and sure of themselves, but they oppressed others and twisted justice. That is why God announces that judgment will come upon them, and the next verse mentions a nation that would oppress them.

For today: let us examine whether in our work, our families, or our church we deal with justice and honesty. Let us ask God not to let comfort harden us to the pain of others.
exp.6:0:
He said that God showed Amos a vision: God himself was forming a swarm of locusts just as the latter growth began to sprout, that is, the grass that comes up at the end of the season. This happened after the king's mowings, probably the first harvest that was handed over to the king. So the new grass was all that was left for the livestock.

Amos speaks as a shepherd and fig farmer from Judah, sent to warn the northern kingdom, Israel. The vision shows a judgment that was approaching because of the people's injustice. The verses that follow show that Amos interceded, and God decided not to send that punishment. Some understand the locusts to be real and others to be a symbolic image; the text does not make this clear.

Today we can imitate Amos: when we see sin and its consequences, we can pray for others with humility, asking for mercy and not only judgment.
exp.6:3:
God showed the prophet Amos a second vision: the Lord called for judgment by fire, and the fire was so great that it swallowed up the deep waters beneath the earth and began to burn part of the land.

The fire devoured the great deep completely, and it ate up a part of the land.

Amos, a shepherd whom God sent as a prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel, speaks here. Earlier he saw the plague of locusts; now he sees the fire. The people were living in injustice and had turned away from God, and so the judgment was real. Even so, Amos pleads on behalf of Israel, and God changes course.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also hears prayer. When you see injustice or suffering around you, pray for your family, your community, and your country, asking for mercy as Amos did.
exp.6:7:
God asks Amos what he sees, and he answers: a mason's plumb line. It is a cord with a weight that is used to check whether a wall is straight. God says he will set that plumb line in the midst of his people Israel and that he will no longer pass by them without judgment; he will no longer let them go unpunished.

God speaks through a vision that the prophet Amos receives. Earlier, Amos had interceded, and God changed his mind about other punishments. Now God measures Israel by a straight standard, and the people do not prove to be upright. The altars and the house of King Jeroboam will be affected, and that is why the priest Amaziah becomes angry with Amos.

For today: God does not measure us by appearances, but by his truth. Ask him to examine your life, and humbly correct whatever is crooked before it piles up.
exp.6:8:
He says that God will destroy the places of worship of Israel. The high places and the sanctuaries refer to the religious sites of the people, and the word for being left in ruins means they will be laid waste. Furthermore, God says he will rise up against the house of King Jeroboam, that is, he will bring judgment on their ruling family. Here "Isaac" is used as another name for the people of Israel.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Amos, in a vision of the plumb line. Just as a plumb line measures whether a wall is straight, God measures his people and finds them crooked because of their injustice and idolatry. For this reason he announces judgment. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, responded by accusing Amos before the king.

Today we can let the Word of God be our plumb line. Instead of defending our religion or our habits, it is wise to ask ourselves humbly whether our lives are straight before him, and to correct our course in time.
exp.6:9:
Amaziah, the priest of Beth-el, sends a message to King Jeroboam. He says that Amos has conspired against the king, meaning that Amos is plotting or scheming something against him. He adds that the land is not able to bear Amos's words, that is, that the country can no longer put up with them.

Amaziah was the priest of the sanctuary at Beth-el, a place of worship that the northern kingdom used and that the king supported. Amos, a prophet who had come from Judah, had just announced God's judgment on that worship and on the king's house. Amaziah does not report everything accurately: Amos spoke on behalf of God, not as part of a plot. Amaziah presents him as a political threat.

When the Word of God makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to accuse the messenger instead of examining our own hearts. Let us pray for humility to listen to the truth, even when it hurts.
exp.7:2:
God announces that the temple singers, instead of singing, will cry out in loud wailing when judgment comes. There will be many dead bodies lying everywhere, with no funeral and in silence. Some translations say it is "the songs of the temple" that will turn into lament; the Hebrew allows both readings.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. He has just shown him a basket of ripe fruit, a sign that Israel is ripe for judgment. The reason is given in the verses that follow: the rich were exploiting the poor, cheating with the measures, and eagerly waiting for the day of rest to end so they could go back to selling.

For today: worship is worth nothing if we live alongside injustice. Examine how you treat those who depend on you, in your work or in your business, and be honest and fair with them.
exp.7:4:
It says that some impatient merchants complain that the feasts pass very slowly. They want the month to end (the new moon) and the week (the sabbath) to be over so they can go back to selling. The storehouses, where the grain is kept, are their base of operations. Their plan is to make the measure smaller, raise the price, and rig the scales to deceive.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, in the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses the rich who appear to be religious but oppress the poor. The days of rest were meant to honor God, and they thought only about earning money. For this reason God promises judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith shows in our work and in our business dealings. Let us practice honesty: giving a fair price, paying well, and not taking advantage of those who have less.
exp.7:5:
They said that some merchants wanted to buy the poor for money, and the needy for the price of a pair of shoes, that is, for very little. They also wanted to sell the sweepings of the wheat, which are the waste, the chaff and the bad grain left after cleaning wheat, as if it were good product.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, in the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses the rich who waited impatiently for the days of religious rest to end so they could get back to their business. They used false weights and raised prices. The poor, in debt, ended up enslaved over small debts. God says he will not forget these deeds.

For today: check whether in your work or your business you deal justly with those who have less power. Pay what is fair, do not cheat, and do not take advantage of others' need. Your faith shows in how you treat the vulnerable.
exp.7:10:
Here God announces that days will come when there will be a hunger very different from hunger in the stomach: there will be no lack of bread or water, but a lack of hearing the words of the Lord. "Hearing" means listening, and "the words of the Lord" refers to his message and his guidance.

God himself speaks through the prophet Amos, who directed his message to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. The people lived with injustice, mistreated the poor, and kept up a religion that was only for show. God had already spoken to them and they did not want to listen. For this reason he warns that a time of silence and judgment will come, with sorrow and a fruitless search. Scholars do not agree on exactly when this was fulfilled.

Today we can value the Bible while we still have it at hand. A practical idea: set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage calmly and to act on something specific that God shows you.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that in the days God announces, even the young and strong, the beautiful young women and the young men, will faint from thirst. This thirst is not for water, but for hearing the word of God, as the verse before it says.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to Israel, the northern kingdom. The people lived with injustice and false religion, and had ignored God's messages. So he warns them that a time would come when they would seek his word and not find it. Those who swear by idols, like those of Samaria and Dan, will fall.

Today we can value the Bible while we have it at hand. Let us not leave it for later: let us read a little each day, with a heart ready to obey.
exp.8:2:
It says that no one can hide from God. Even if someone flees to the top of Mount Carmel, which was a high place with caves and a lot of vegetation, God will search for them and catch them there. And if they sank to the bottom of the sea, God would command the serpent (a snake, perhaps a sea creature) to bite them. "Them" here refers to those who are hiding.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. The people lived in injustice, mistreated the poor, and practiced an empty religion. God announces a judgment from which no one will escape. Some think the vision of the altar refers to the sanctuary at Bethel, but the text does not fully make this clear.

Today, this verse reminds us that we cannot deceive God or flee from Him. If there is something we are hiding, the best thing is to come to Him with sincerity, ask forgiveness, and change. His gaze is also a comfort to those who seek Him with their whole heart.
exp.8:3:
It says that even if the people are taken away as captives and live among their enemies, they will not escape God's judgment. God himself commands that they be struck down by the sword. The phrase about setting his eyes on them means that his gaze, which once watched over his people, now watches to bring punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel, which lived in injustice, oppressed the poor, and practiced an empty religion. They believed that because they were the chosen people, they were safe. God warns them that nothing and no one will rescue them. But the book ends with a promise of restoration.

For today: do not confuse God's grace with permission to live as you please. Examine your life honestly, give up what you know displeases him, and seek justice and mercy toward others.
exp.8:4:
The Lord God of hosts has power over the whole earth. When he merely touches it, it melts, and all who live in it mourn. The land rises up like a river that swells and then sinks back down, just as the Nile does in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the kingdom of Israel, which lived in injustice and false security. Earlier he said that no one could hide from his judgment. This verse shows that nothing is too firm before God, not even the earth itself. Some see here a poetic image of judgment, and others think of a real earthquake or flood; the text does not make this clear.

For today: let us not trust in our security, money, or strength, but in God. Let us live with humility, doing justice and seeking his forgiveness.
exp.8:7:
He says that God sees everything and has his eyes on the sinful kingdom, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, which lived in injustice. He will destroy it and wipe it from the face of the earth, meaning its surface. But he promises that he will not completely finish off the house of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who warns Israel in a time of comfort and sin. The people believed their relationship with God protected them from all punishment. God reminds them that his favor is not a permission to sin. Even so, in the midst of judgment, he leaves a hope open.

For today: God is just and takes us seriously, but he is also faithful and merciful. Do not use his grace as an excuse to live badly. If you have failed, return to him, because his discipline seeks to restore you, not destroy you.
exp.8:8:
For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.

God says that He Himself will command that the people of Israel be shaken among all the nations, the way grain is shaken in a large sieve. When it is shaken, the chaff and the small stones come out, but not a single good grain that falls to the ground is lost.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. Israel believed it could not be touched because it was the chosen people, but God reminds them that He also guides other nations. Because of their sin, judgment and scattering will come, but God promises not to destroy the house of Jacob completely. The proud sinners will fall, and afterward God will restore.

For today: when you go through trials or corrections, remember that God does not shake you to destroy you, but to purify you. Examine your heart with humility and trust that He cares for what is His.
exp.8:11:
He says that God will restore his people so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations over which his name has been called. Edom is the neighboring people and enemy of Israel. "Possess" means to inherit or take part in something. Some understand "the remnant of Edom" to mean the people who are left of that nation.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. He has just announced judgment on the proud sinners among his people, but he promises to raise up the fallen house of David. In Acts 15:16-17, James quotes this passage (according to the Greek version) to show that the Gentiles also seek the Lord.

For today: God does not leave permanently fallen the things he decides to restore. Trust his promise and open your heart to people who are different from you, because his grace is for everyone.
exp.8:14:
God promises to plant his people in their own land, like someone planting a tree with firm roots. He says they will never again be uprooted from the land he has given them.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who earlier announced judgment on Israel for its injustice and idolatry. But the book ends with hope: God will restore what has been destroyed. Some believe this was fulfilled in part with the return from exile; others see it fulfilled in Christ and his Church, and others expect a future fulfillment. Christians understand it in different ways.

For today: even when you have failed or feel you have lost everything, God remains faithful to his promises. Trust that he is able to restore and re-establish your life. Return to him sincerely.
exp.1:8:
The explanation says that God destroyed the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan before Israel. They are described as tall and strong, as tall as cedars and as strong as oaks. "I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below" means that God removed them completely, from the highest part to the deepest.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. He reminds them that he gave them the land by defeating a people who seemed unbeatable. He does this because they now oppress the poor, abuse the weak, and dishonor his name. Their ingratitude is all the more serious because God had cared for them.

For today: Remember what God has done for you, and let that gratitude lead you to treat the weakest people around you with justice and kindness.
exp.6:6:
He says God showed Amos a vision: the Lord was standing beside a wall that was true to plumb, meaning perfectly straight, and in his hand he held a plumb line. A plumb line is a cord with a weight that builders use to check whether a wall is upright. The word for "showed" in the original is the same as the word that appears in the verse above, "showed."

Amos, a prophet of the 8th century B.C., speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel. He had already interceded for the people in two earlier visions, and God had relented from punishing them. Now God uses the plumb line as a measure: Israel is crooked, and this time he will not overlook its sin. Many understand the wall as an image of the people, though the text leaves it as a symbol.

God measures our lives by his truth, not by our excuses. We can ask him to show us, with patience, where we have gone crooked, and to repent in time, trusting in his grace.
exp.4:7:
He tells us to look to God, who made the Pleiades and Orion, who turns darkness into dawn and day into night, and who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth. His name is the LORD. The exact identities of the stars named here are uncertain, though the Pleiades and Orion are the names this translation gives.

The prophet Amos, sent by God to the northern kingdom of Israel, speaks here to the people he calls the house of Joseph. The people were practicing injustice, and Amos calls them to seek God before judgment comes. Reminding them who God is shows that He has power over all things and cannot be ignored.

Today, before we worry over our own plans, we can look at the sky and remember that God governs all things. That reverence invites us to seek Him and to treat others with justice.
exp.4:6:
There are people who turn justice into something bitter, so that the courts become a source of pain for those who seek fairness. The "wormwood" is a plant with a very bitter taste, a symbol of suffering. And when the verse says they cast righteousness to the ground, it means they throw justice down and trample it, showing no respect for it.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who brought his message to the kingdom of Israel. The people practiced a religion full of visits to sanctuaries such as Bethel and Gilgal, yet in daily life there was injustice against the poor. God calls them to seek Him, not only to attend religious places.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat others. If we have any power, at work, in the family or in the community, we can ask ourselves whether we use it with honesty and justice, especially toward those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.2:10:
This verse announces a punishment. God says that an enemy will surround the land, pull down Israel's strongholds, and plunder its citadels. "Plunder" means that everything they had stored up will be taken from them by force.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, whose capital was Samaria. The verses before this one say that the rich were piling up wealth through violence and oppression, and that they did not know how to do what is right. That is why the judgment comes right where they kept their treasures. The text does not name the enemy; later history connects it with Assyria.

For today: riches and security gained by harming others are not firm. Today we can examine how we earn and use what we have, and ask God to help us act with justice and compassion.
exp.4:16:
Amos 5:17 says there will be wailing in all the vineyards, places that once meant joy, hard work, and harvest. Where there used to be celebration, there will now be mourning. God himself announces, "I will pass through your midst," meaning he will come among his people to judge them. A lament is a sad song sung at a funeral.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel. The people lived with injustice and a false sense of security in their religion. The image of God passing through recalls the Passover in Egypt, when the Lord passed through to judge, but now the judgment falls on his own people. Even so, there was an earlier invitation: "hate evil and love good."

For today: let us not confuse closeness to God with a life that never changes. This week, examine one area where you treat others poorly or ignore justice, and decide to correct it with humility.
exp.8:0:
Amos reports that he saw the Lord standing beside the altar. God gives a command: strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake, and bring the structure down on all the people. "The rest" will be killed by the sword, and no one will be able to run away. Those who flee will not get away, and those who try to escape will not be spared.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who delivered his message to the kingdom of Israel. Many believe the temple in view was the one at Bethel, although the text does not state this clearly. The people kept up a religion that was only for show, yet they committed injustices and oppressed the poor. For this reason God announces judgment.

Today: God is not fooled by a religion that is only for show. Ask him to examine your heart, and let your faith be seen in your honesty and in fair dealing with others. At the end of the book, God also promises restoration.
exp.1:1:
God says he will send fire against Moab, and that fire will consume the citadels of Kerioth, a Moabite city. Moab will fall in tumult, amid war cries and the sound of the ram's horn. The words "tumult" and "war cries" describe a great uproar and the noise of battle. "Consume" means the fire will destroy the city completely.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos, who announces judgment on several nations neighboring Israel. God punishes Moab because it burned the bones of the king of Edom until they became lime, an act of contempt toward a dead man. The historical details of that event are not known with certainty. Even so, the text shows that God holds all nations accountable.

For today: God sees cruelty and contempt, even when no one else sees them. Today we can ask him to teach us to treat everyone with respect, even those we consider enemies.
exp.7:6:
God makes a solemn oath: he swears "by the Pride of Jacob," a phrase that is understood in different ways. Some think it refers to Israel's own pride; others take it to mean God himself, as the glory of his people. What is clear is the message: "I will never forget any of their deeds." It refers to the injustices he has just described.

Amos was a shepherd from Judah whom God sent to speak to the northern kingdom, Israel. The merchants were impatient for the days of religious rest to end so they could go back to selling, cheat with false weights, and exploit the poor. Meanwhile, they pretended to be pious. God answers that he sees everything.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are honest in our work and business, and whether we treat fairly those who have less power than we do. God does not forget what we do, and he also has compassion on whoever cries out to him.
exp.6:4:
In this verse, the prophet Amos pleads with God to stop the punishment. The word "stop" in the verse means "stop" or "end." The reason he gives is that Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, is so small that they could not survive such a blow.

The speaker is Amos, a prophet of the eighth century B.C., who sees visions of God's judgment on Israel for its injustice. Before this vision, God had shown him a plague of locusts and also held it back when Amos interceded. Here it is a fire that consumes the land, and again God relents, that is, changes his decision. Some understand this as a human way of describing God's compassion.

For today: we can pray for others with boldness, as Amos did, asking for mercy for those who are weak or who have fallen short, trusting that God listens and is compassionate.
exp.4:12:
Amos 5:13 says that the wise keep quiet in times like these, because the days are evil. This verse describes a person who is careful and discerning, and who recognizes that in a time of great wrongdoing, speaking may be useless or dangerous.

The prophet Amos, sent by God to the kingdom of Israel, is the speaker here. He charges the rich with oppressing the poor, taking bribes, and denying justice at the gate, the place where legal cases were decided. Some readers take the silence as a criticism of a society where speaking out was pointless or risky. Others understand it as advice about prudence. The verses that follow call people to seek good, so silence does not seem to be what God asks of them.

For today: before you speak, ask for wisdom to know when to be silent and when to stand up for the needy with courage and respect.
exp.3:11:
God tells Israel that he is going to act against them, and so he calls on them to prepare, or get ready, to meet him. The explanation does not say exactly what "this" refers to, but the wording makes clear that a serious judgment is coming.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier in the book he has recalled plagues, war and destruction, and he now says that, even so, the people did not return to him. Some read the call as a warning to turn back while there is still time; others read it as an announcement of judgment that cannot be avoided. The text allows both readings.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when God speaks to us, not even through difficulties. Today you can stop, pray sincerely, and correct what you know he is pointing out to you, without waiting for everything to become more complicated.
exp.7:11:
The verse says the people will stagger from sea to sea and roam from north to east, searching for a word from God, but they will not find it. "Stagger" means they stumble about, lost and without direction. "Roam" means they keep moving from place to place, looking for something they cannot reach.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who announced judgment on the northern kingdom, Israel. The people lived in injustice, mistreated the poor, and had a religion that was only for show. God had sent prophets, but they would not listen. Now he warns that a time of silence will come: not a hunger for bread, but a lack of his word.

For today: let us not neglect the Bible while we have it close at hand. Let us read it calmly and with a desire to obey, before urgency makes us look for it too late. God speaks today; let us listen with a willing heart.
exp.4:23:
God wants justice in decisions and in how people treat one another to keep flowing without stopping, like a river, and righteousness to be like an ever-flowing stream that never runs dry. "Instead" is the sense of the opening word "But" here. "Ever-flowing" means strong and constant.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the people of Israel. They offered many sacrifices and sang at their festivals, but they lived with injustice and also worshiped other gods. For this reason God rejects their religion, which was only for show. Some scholars think the verses that follow speak of ancient idolatry; the details of those names are interpreted in various ways.

For today: attending church or singing with enthusiasm is not enough. Ask yourself where you can act justly this week: paying what is fair, not lying at work, or standing up for someone who is being mistreated.
exp.4:4:
God tells the Israelites not to go looking for him at Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba. These were places where people went to worship. Bethel is the place the text calls Bethel, and Beersheba is the place it calls Beersheba. The message is harsh: Gilgal will be taken into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing, meaning it will be destroyed and reduced to ruin.

The prophet Amos speaks on behalf of the LORD to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people practiced a great deal of religion at these shrines, but they lived unjustly, as the verses that follow show. God calls them to seek him, not the places, and promises them: "Seek me, and you shall live." The coming destruction would show that these sites could not save them.

For today: do not trust in rituals, places, or religious customs as if they were a guarantee before God. Seek him with your whole heart, and let your faith show in how you treat others with justice.
exp.3:1:
God himself makes a solemn oath, resting on his holiness, that is, on his perfect character. He announces that days are coming when these women will be taken away with hooks, as fish are caught, and their descendants with fishhooks. The image speaks of a humiliating capture. Some scholars think it describes how the Assyrians led away captives; others understand it in a more general way.

Amos, a shepherd sent by God, speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel. He calls the wealthy women of Samaria "cows of Bashan," women who lived well while they oppressed the poor and urged their husbands to bring them drink. God confronts them for that injustice.

For today: God sees how we treat the weak. Let us examine whether our comfort rests on the suffering of others, and seek to be just and generous.
exp.4:2:
God says that a great loss is coming for Israel. A city that marches out a thousand strong will have only a hundred left, and the one that marches out a hundred strong will have only ten left in the house of Israel. The phrase "marches out" tells us these groups are setting out to fight. In other words, almost all of them will die, and every city will be left very weak.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, who sings a funeral song of mourning over Israel, the northern kingdom. God denounces the people's injustice and their false religion. Even so, in the next verse he leaves a door open: "Seek me, and you shall live." The judgment is serious, but the invitation still stands.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, our numbers, or our religious habits. What gives life is truly seeking God, with humility and obedience. Right now, ask him to show you something you need to correct, and answer him without delay.
exp.5:13:
God says that he will send a nation to oppress Israel. "I will raise up a nation against you" means that God himself will bring about this enemy people. "They will oppress you" means that they will rule over you harshly. "From Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah" marks the boundaries of the kingdom: from north to south, the whole territory would be affected.

God speaks through the prophet Amos. Israel lived in comfort and pride, trusting in its own strength, while it twisted justice and mistreated the weak. For this reason God announces judgment. Many understand the invading people to be Assyria, although the text does not name it here.

For today: let us not trust in our achievements or our strength, as if they were our security. Let us examine with humility whether we practice justice in how we treat others, and ask God to teach us to live with honesty and compassion.
exp.4:0:
Hear this word, the prophet says, and listen closely to what is coming. The word "lamentation" refers to a funeral song, a mourning cry sung for the dead. Amos speaks as if Israel were already in mourning, even though the nation was still alive.

Amos, a shepherd from Judah sent by God, speaks to the northern kingdom, the house of Israel. This took place in a time of prosperity, but also of injustice and idolatry. The verses that follow say that Israel would fall and be greatly reduced. God warns sternly because he wants the people to respond and return to him.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings, even when everything seems to be going well. If his Word points out something in your life, listen with humility and change in time. God's correction seeks to save us, not to destroy us.
exp.5:3:
It says that some people live in great luxury and comfort. They lie on beds inlaid with ivory, they lounge upon their couches, and they dine on the best food: lambs from the flock and calves from the stall, raised apart to be fattened for the table. The "stall" is the place where livestock is kept and fattened. The "couches" are the beds or sofas where they reclined.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, Israel. The leaders felt secure and prosperous, but they ignored the injustice and suffering of the people. God does not condemn having possessions in themselves, but the indifference, because the ruin of Joseph, that is, of Israel, did not grieve them.

Today, God invites us to examine whether comfort has made us indifferent. We can ask ourselves who near us is suffering and what we can do, through prayer, time, or concrete help, to stand with them.
exp.1:9:
God reminds the Israelites that it was He who brought them out of Egypt and led them forty years through the wilderness. All of that had a purpose: that they would take possession of the land of the Amorite, the people who lived in Canaan.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, who addresses the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier, God accuses them of injustice and idolatry. Here He reminds them of His faithfulness in the past to show that their sin is ingratitude. They received everything by grace, not by their own merit.

For today: remember what God has done in your life, the times He sustained you or opened a way for you. A grateful memory helps us live with humility, obey with joy, and treat others justly.
exp.5:12:
The verse says that some people rejoice in something that is really worth nothing. The phrase "you who rejoice in Lo-debar" points to a worthless achievement, since Lo-debar was a town of no real value. They also boast, "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?", meaning they credit their own power for winning Karnaim. Karnaim was a place whose name carries the idea of horns, a symbol of strength, and many believe Amos is playing on those names.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to the kingdom of Israel, which was prosperous but unjust. The verses before this one accuse them of turning justice into poison and righteousness into bitterness. God warns them that their pride will end when a foreign people oppresses them.

Today we might ask ourselves what we boast about: money, success or ability. All of that amounts to little if we achieve it without justice and without depending on God. Let us be thankful for what we have and deal fairly with others.
exp.6:16:
This verse is God's judgment against Amaziah, the priest of Bethel. It says that his wife would be made a prostitute in the city, that his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, and that his land would be divided up by a measuring line. He himself would die on pagan soil, and Israel would surely go into exile, away from its homeland. The word "prostitute" is usually understood as forced prostitution or disgrace after an invasion, though some explain it in other ways.

The Lord speaks through Amos, a shepherd and grower of figs from Judah. Amaziah had ordered him to be silent and go back to his own country because his warnings were troubling the king. Amos answers that he does not speak on his own authority, but because God sent him. To reject the prophet was to reject God.

For today: when God's Word makes us uncomfortable, let us not silence it or defend ourselves against it. Let us listen with humility and allow it to correct us in time.
exp.2:9:
The explanation says that the people of Samaria no longer know how to act with justice. "Doing right" means acting in what is correct and fair. "Violence" is harm done by force, and "destruction" is the ruin that follows. Their citadels were full of wealth gained by harming others.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel, whose capital was Samaria. God calls as witnesses Ashdod and Egypt so that they may see the oppression and violence within the city. Therefore, in the verses that follow, he announces that an enemy will come and tear down those same strongholds.

For today: God looks at how we obtain what we have, not only at how much we have. We can ask ourselves whether our money, work, or businesses treat other people with justice and honesty.
exp.7:0:
God showed the prophet Amos a vision: a basket of ripe fruit, the kind gathered at the end of summer. "The Lord GOD" is the name of God, and a basket is a small, shallow container. On its own, the image seems calm and even pleasant.

Amos is a shepherd and a farmer whom God sent to speak to the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. He speaks in the first person and tells what God shows him. In the original language, the words for "summer fruit" sound close to the word for "end," and many scholars see a wordplay there. Just as ripe fruit does not last long, God's patience with the people's injustice was reaching its limit.

For today: God is patient, but he does not ignore injustice. We should not take his patience as permission to keep doing wrong. Today we can repent and treat others with justice.
exp.1:15:
It says that even the bravest of the mighty men will flee naked on that day, declared the LORD. "Bravest" in the verse means the most courageous, strong in spirit. "Naked" probably indicates that he will leave everything behind, even his armor, in order to escape.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who announced judgment on the kingdom of Israel, in the north. God rebuked them for injustice, the oppression of the poor, and false worship. Here he describes a day of defeat in which no one, not even the most skilled soldier, will be saved by his own strength.

For today: our strength, talent, or position does not shield us from being accountable before God. Instead of trusting in ourselves, we can act with justice and humility, and seek his mercy today.
exp.2:6:
God does not act by surprise. Before doing something important, he makes his plan known to the prophets, who are his servants. The word "plan" here means his purpose, what he has decided to do. "Revealing" means that he makes it known.

The prophet Amos speaks, a shepherd from Judah sent to warn the northern kingdom, Israel. Before this verse, he asks questions that show every effect has a cause. So the judgment that comes upon Israel for its oppression and violence is not chance. God had already warned them, and that is why Amos cannot keep silent.

For today: God speaks with clarity, so it is wise to listen to his Word with humility and respond in time. If there is something in your life that the Bible shows you should correct, do not put it off; God warns you because he wants to help you.
exp.3:0:
God calls certain women of Samaria "cows of Bashan." Bashan was a region known for its well-fed cattle. These women oppress the poor and crush the needy. They also say to their husbands, "Bring us more to drink."

The prophet Amos, sent by God to the kingdom of Israel, is speaking. Its capital was Samaria. It was a time of wealth and luxury, but also of great injustice. The verses that follow announce judgment: the people will be led away captive. Some think the insult is aimed at upper-class women; others, at the whole ruling class.

For today: God sees how we use what we have. Let us examine whether our comfort rests on the expense of others, and look for a concrete way to help someone in need this week.
exp.4:24:
God asks Israel a question: "Did you bring me sacrifices and offerings during the forty years in the wilderness?" The question can be understood in two ways: that Israel did not offer faithful sacrifices in that time, or that what mattered then was not the rituals but the obedience of the heart. Scholars interpret it in both ways.

God speaks through the prophet Amos. He rebukes a people who sang and offered sacrifices but practiced injustice. The verses that follow say that they also carried idols, and for this reason he announces that they would be taken into exile.

For today: God is not satisfied with songs and religious activities if the heart is far from Him. Today we can ask ourselves whether our worship is reflected in how we treat others, with honesty, justice and mercy.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that no one can hide from God. The Berean Standard Bible renders the place of the dead as Sheol, the realm of the dead, the deepest point imaginable. "Heaven" is the highest point. Digging down or climbing up does not help: God's hand reaches everywhere.

God himself is speaking, shown to Amos in a vision beside the altar. Amos was prophesying to the northern kingdom, Israel, which lived with injustice, the oppression of the poor, and an empty religion. God announces judgment and says that no one will escape the consequences of their rebellion.

For today: we cannot hide anything from God, so it is wise to live with sincerity. If something weighs on you, do not conceal it; bring it honestly to him, trusting that his mercy also reaches the one who repents.
exp.0:4:
God says he will break down the gates of Damascus, the capital of Aram, which is Syria. In the original picture, the gates were guarded by a great bar, a heavy bolt that stood for the city's protection, so breaking it means its defenses will fall. "Cut off" means wiped out or destroyed. The places named here, the Valley of Aven and Beth-eden, were locations within the kingdom, and the "ruler" and the one who "wields the scepter" were the men who held power there. Scholars are not sure exactly where these places were. The people of Aram will be "exiled to Kir," taken away from their land, and Kir is a region whose exact location is also debated.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. He announces this judgment because Damascus treated Gilead, a neighboring people of Israel, with terrible cruelty, threshing them with iron threshing instruments, an image of brutal violence. God does not overlook the injustice of the nations.

For today: no human power, wealth, or influence can shield us from the justice of God. We can trust that he sees abuse, and we can examine whether we treat the weak with respect and kindness.
exp.0:2:
God says he will not let Damascus, the capital of Syria (Aram), go unpunished. The phrase "for three transgressions, even four" is a way of speaking that shows the wickedness has reached its limit. Threshing was passing a heavy sledge over grain to separate it from the straw; here it describes brutal cruelty against Gilead, a region of Israel east of the Jordan. "I will not revoke my judgment" means he will not take back or hold back the punishment.

The Lord speaks through Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam. Before speaking about Israel, God begins by judging the neighboring nations. In this way he shows that he is judge of all peoples and that violence against others matters to him. The exact historical details of that cruelty are not explained here; the text presents it as the language of cruel warfare.

For today: God sees the mistreatment of the weak and does not ignore it. We can ask him to make us compassionate and to reject any harsh treatment of others, even when it seems normal.
exp.6:15:
Amos tells Amaziah to listen to what the Lord has to say. He reminds him of what the priest had ordered: not to prophesy against Israel or to preach against "the house of Isaac," another way of naming the people of Israel, descended from Isaac.

Amaziah was a priest at Bethel, where the king had his sanctuary, and he had ordered Amos to be silent. Amos, a shepherd and grower of figs whom God called, answers with firmness. Now the message is no longer only about the nation but becomes a personal judgment against Amaziah for having wanted to silence the word of God.

For today: let us not fear the truth of God, even when it is uncomfortable. Let us hear his Word with humility, and if we speak of it, let us do so with respect and courage, without allowing human pressures to silence it.
exp.6:2:
It says that God relented from what he was going to do: he would not send the plague of locusts upon the people. The words "It will not happen" are his decision to stop the punishment. Here "relented" does not mean that God was wrong, but that he changed course and showed compassion.

The prophet Amos speaks, recounting a vision that God showed him. The locusts were going to eat the grass that remained after the king's harvest, something that would have brought hunger. Amos pleaded: "Lord GOD, forgive, I beg You! How can Jacob survive? He is so small." God heard his plea and stopped the judgment.

For today: God hears the prayer of one who intercedes for others. We can ask for mercy for our family, church, or nation, trusting that God is compassionate and does not delight in punishing.
exp.1:2:
God says that he will remove the ruler of Moab, the leader who governs and rules over the people. Together with him, he will kill all the officials who serve under him. The old-wording note about "I will slay" is not needed here, since the verse above already uses plain modern words for these ideas.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. Earlier he has said that Moab burned the bones of the king of Edom until they became lime, an act of contempt toward someone who had died. God judges cruelty even among nations that did not have his law. Moab will lose its leaders and fall in war.

For today: God takes notice of how we treat even those we regard as enemies, including people who can no longer defend themselves. Today we can ask him to give us a just heart that is respectful toward everyone, and to pray for our leaders so that they govern with justice.
exp.4:5:
He says Israel must seek God in order to live. If they do not, God's judgment will sweep through like a fire that spreads and consumes everything. The picture is of a fire that moves quickly through a house and burns it all, with no one at Bethel able to put it out. The "house of Joseph" refers to the northern kingdom, Israel, whose main tribes descended from Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh).

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Amos. He calls the people to turn to Him and not to famous places of worship, such as Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. Israel trusted in its religion, but lived in injustice, and God warns them that those places will not save them.

For today: seeking God is not just attending a religious place or following customs. It means coming to Him with sincerity, and living with justice and humility. Today you can ask yourself: what do I trust more, my religious routines or God Himself?
exp.0:14:
This verse says that the king of Ammon will be taken away as a prisoner to another land, together with all his princes. "Exile" means being forced to leave one's own country and live far away. At the end appears the phrase "says the LORD," which shows that it is God who declares it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Amos. He is judging Ammon, a people neighboring Israel, for a terrible cruelty: attacking pregnant women in Gilead in order to enlarge their territory. Its leaders were responsible for that violent ambition. Some scholars think that "their king" could also be understood as the god Milcom, since the Hebrew word is similar, but this is debated.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. Whoever has authority should use it to care for the weak, not to take advantage of them.
exp.0:10:
God says he will not overlook the sins of Edom. The phrase "for three transgressions, even four" is a way of saying that their wickedness had reached its full measure. Edom pursued his brother with the sword. The explanation says he stifled all compassion. His anger raged without stopping, and his fury burned without end.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, who pronounces judgment on the nations around Israel. Edom descended from Esau, brother of Jacob, so his cruelty was against his own family. God judges violence and the refusal to show mercy, and the punishment is stated right after in the text.

For today: resentment held on to year after year hardens the heart. If there is someone you hold anger against, ask God for help to forgive and, if possible, to seek reconciliation.
exp.3:2:
The verse says that the wealthy women of Samaria will leave the city through the broken walls, each one going straight ahead, and that they will be driven out toward Harmon. The breaks in the walls are the gaps or cracks where the defenses have fallen apart, and the women will pass through them one after another in a line. The LORD himself declares that this will happen. Scholars are not fully sure of the exact location named as Harmon, so the place itself remains uncertain.

The prophet Amos speaks God's message to the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BC. He calls the upper-class women who lived in luxury, oppressed the poor, and urged their husbands to bring more drink "cows of Bashan." God announces judgment for that injustice, even though they continued to take part in their religious practices.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the needy. We can ask ourselves whether our comfort depends on ignoring or taking advantage of others, and look for a concrete way to help others with justice and compassion.
exp.1:11:
It says that the people of Israel made the Nazirites, people set apart for God who were not to drink wine, break their vow by giving them wine. It also ordered the prophets to be silent, telling them: "Do not prophesy," that is, "do not speak on God's behalf."

God speaks through the prophet Amos. He reminds them that He brought them out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and gave them the land. He also gave them prophets and Nazirites as gifts to guide them. Now they reject them, and therefore the judgment announced in the following verses is coming.

For today: God speaks to us in many ways, and sometimes His message is uncomfortable. We can ask ourselves whether we silence God's voice because it bothers us. A humble attitude is to listen to His Word, even when it corrects us, and to support those who try to live faithfully for Him.
exp.1:10:
God says that, besides giving them the land, he also raised up some among the children of Israel as prophets, to speak to them on his behalf, and some of their young men as Nazirites, people set apart for God who did not drink wine or cut their hair. Then he asks, "Is this not true?", as one who asks them to recognize what is plain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, in the northern kingdom. He reminds them of his past kindness: defeating the Amorites, bringing them out of Egypt, and guiding them through the wilderness. But the people responded badly: they made the Nazirites drink wine and ordered the prophets to be silent. Because of this, judgment is coming.

For today: God still gives voices and examples of faith around us. Let us listen humbly to biblical correction and value those who live with integrity, instead of silencing or discouraging them.
exp.8:13:
God promises to reverse the fortunes of his people. "I will restore My people Israel from captivity" means bringing them back from exile and returning what they lost. The cities that lie in ruin will be rebuilt and lived in again. They will plant vineyards and make gardens, and they will drink the wine and eat the fruit. It is a picture of an ordinary life, settled and at peace.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. Throughout the book he announces judgment on Israel for its injustice and idolatry. But it ends with hope: after the punishment, God will restore his people. Some see here the return from exile, others a future restoration, and others a spiritual fulfillment in Christ. Christians have understood this passage in different ways.

For today: God does not leave his own in ruin. If you are going through a loss or a failure, trust that he can rebuild your life. Return to him and take one small step of rebuilding today.
exp.3:3:
God says, with irony: "Go to Bethel and keep sinning; at Gilgal, rebel even more." Going against the truth and what is right is the sense of the word translated here as "transgress." The verse speaks of bringing sacrifices every morning and tithes every three days, that is, keeping their religious practices with great zeal.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, who addresses the northern kingdom, Israel. Bethel and Gilgal were well-known places of worship, but there the people mixed religion with injustice and disobedience. The words are sarcastic: God does not approve those rites, because their hearts remained far from him. The verses before this one announce judgment.

For today: performing rituals is not enough, such as attending church or giving offerings, if we live without justice and obedience. Let us ask God for a sincere heart that truly seeks him.
exp.6:1:
When the locusts had eaten every green plant in the land, Amos cried out to God: "Lord GOD, please forgive! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?" The phrase "please forgive" is an urgent plea, and "Jacob" stands for the people of Israel.

The prophet Amos speaks here and recounts a vision that God showed him. The locusts destroy the late harvest, and this pictures a judgment coming upon Israel because of its sin. Amos does not defend the people by claiming they are innocent. Instead he appeals to God's mercy, because Israel was weak. The following verse says that God "relented," a statement showing that He answered the prayer and stopped that punishment.

For today: when you see the failure or the frailty of others, pray for them as Amos did, asking for mercy instead of merely criticizing.
exp.3:6:
God says that he held back the rain three months before the harvest, just when the crops most needed it for the grain to ripen. He sent rain on one city but withheld it from another, so one field received rain while another without rain withered.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. The people were religious on the outside, but they lived with injustice. God sent them famine, drought and plagues to call them back to himself. After each punishment he says, "yet you have not returned to me."

Today we can ask whether certain difficulties invite us to draw near to God. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but every difficulty is a good moment to examine the heart and return to him with sincerity, not just with rituals.
exp.4:26:
God says: "I will send you into exile beyond Damascus." Exile means being taken away from your land and forced to live somewhere else. The one speaking is the LORD, called "the God of hosts," that is, the Lord of all power.
