Amos speaks on God's behalf to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. The people kept up a religion full of rituals, but they also worshiped idols. The names of the idols mentioned in this passage are not fully clear, so it is not known for certain which gods they refer to. That is why God announces exile as the consequence of their unfaithfulness. Later on, history points to Assyria as the power that carried the northern kingdom into exile.

Today we can ask ourselves what truly holds first place in our hearts. God does not seek only religious acts, but a sincere devotion. If something has taken His place, it is wise to return to Him in time.
exp.7:1:
God asks Amos what he sees, and he answers: a basket of ripe summer fruit. Then God says to him that the end has come for His people Israel, and that He will no longer spare them. The phrase "I will no longer spare them" means He will no longer hold back judgment.

The Lord speaks, and Amos is the prophet who listens. In the Hebrew, "summer fruit" and "end" sound alike, and many scholars see a play on words there. Because ripe fruit spoils quickly, Israel was ready for judgment because of its injustice toward the poor, as what follows shows.

Today, God's patience is not indifference. Examine with humility how you treat those in need, and do not postpone change or repentance.
exp.4:8:
God is the one who flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold. A plunderer is someone who seizes what belongs to others. Here, "strong" refers to those who hold power or who feel safe in their defenses. In other words, God can bring down what seemed secure.

The speaker is the prophet Amos, sent by God to the people of Israel, the northern kingdom. He confronts them because they twisted justice, mistreated the poor, and rejected the one who spoke the truth. The verse follows a description of God's power over heaven and earth. Many understand it as announcing judgment through an invading army, though the text gives no further detail here.

For today: no one has true security in their money, their position, or their strength if they live in injustice. Today you can examine how you treat the weakest people around you and seek to be honest and just, even when no one is watching.
exp.4:1:
Israel, called "Virgin Israel" (a poetic way of speaking of a young, beautiful nation that had not yet been conquered), has fallen and will never rise again. She lies abandoned in her own land, with no one to raise her up.

The prophet Amos, sent by God to the northern kingdom, sings a funeral song as if Israel were already dead, in order to shake a people who lived in security while practicing injustice and neglecting God. Many understand that he announces the fall that would come at the hands of Assyria, although the text gives no details here. However, verse 4 opens a door: "Seek me, and you shall live."

For today: let us not trust in our apparent stability. If God shows us an error, let us listen in time and return to Him, because His warning seeks to lead us to life.
exp.0:9:
God says he will send fire on the walls of Tyre, and that the fire will consume its citadels. To "send fire" means to bring destruction, and "consume" means the fire will burn the city's strongholds completely. The walls and citadels stand for the city's strength and wealth.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. Tyre was an important trading city, and God judges it because it handed over whole groups of captives to Edom and disregarded a covenant of brotherhood, meaning a treaty or pact of friendship. Some think this refers to a treaty with Israel, though the text does not give details.

For today: God looks at how we treat others and whether we keep our word. Neither money nor power protects us from being held accountable. Today you can ask yourself whether you keep your commitments and whether you care for those who are at a disadvantage.
exp.0:12:
God says he will punish the Ammonites, the descendants of Ammon, for their repeated sins. "For three transgressions, even four" is a way of saying that their wickedness had reached its full measure. Their crime was ripping open the pregnant women of Gilead, an extreme cruelty, in order to enlarge their territory. "I will not revoke My judgment" means that he will not hold it back.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos, who announces judgment on several nations neighboring Israel. Ammon had attacked Gilead, a region east of the Jordan. God judges not only his own people, but also those who commit brutal violence. Then comes the announcement of fire on Rabbah, its capital, and of the captivity of its king.

For today: God sees cruelty against the most defenseless. It is never right to harm others to gain power or advantage. Today we can defend the weak and ask God to deliver us from the ambition that excuses harm.
exp.2:5:
It says that when a ram's horn sounds in a city, the people tremble. And it asks whether, when calamity comes to a city, the LORD has not caused it. The source's word for "blown" here is rendered simply as "sounds," and its word for the people being stirred up means they are startled and unsettled.

The prophet Amos, a shepherd from Judah, speaks here, sent to warn the kingdom of Israel. He uses questions about cause and effect: if there is a roar, there is prey; if a trap springs shut, something set it off. In this way he shows that the judgment he announces is not chance, but the consequence of the people's injustice. The word translated as "calamity" here refers to disaster or trouble, not to sin; some understand it as God's judgment upon a nation.

For today: when God warns us through His Word, let us take His warning seriously. If something troubles our conscience, let us not ignore it; let us return to Him in humility and correct our course in time.
exp.4:14:
God asks his people for three things: to hate evil, to love good, and to establish justice in the gate. The gates of the city were the place where the elders judged cases. To "establish justice" means to set up what is fair and right. The word "perhaps" shows that God's mercy cannot be demanded; it is asked for with humility. "The remnant of Joseph" refers to what was left of the northern kingdom, Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who denounces injustice and religion without obedience. The rich oppressed the poor, and the judges let themselves be bought. God calls for repentance before the punishment announced in the verses that follow arrives.

For today: ask yourself where you have influence, even a small amount, in your home, your work, or your community. There, choose to be just and honest, and defend those who have no voice.
exp.6:14:
Amos says that God took him from following the flock, that is, while he was tending animals, and told him: "Go, speak to My people Israel." The word "prophesy" in this verse means announcing what God says. The phrase "took me" means that God chose him and set him apart for this task.

Amaziah, priest of Bethel, had told him to be quiet and leave, because the king's sanctuary was there. Amos answers that he is not a prophet by trade and does not come from a school of prophets: he is a shepherd and a grower of wild figs. His authority does not come from an office, but from God's calling.

For today: God can call ordinary people, in simple work, to serve Him. If He gives you something to say or to do, do not depend on titles or on the applause of others. Obey with humility and faithfulness, even when someone tries to silence you.
exp.6:12:
Here the priest Amaziah orders Amos to stop speaking on God's behalf at Bethel. He tells him that this place is the king's sanctuary, that is, the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom, and a principal city of great importance to the nation.

Amaziah was a priest at Bethel and served King Jeroboam. Amos, a shepherd who had come from Judah, had announced judgment because of the people's injustice. Amaziah accused him before the king and now tries to silence him and drive him away. Amos answers that he does not speak for a position or for his own gain, but because God himself called him.

For today: let us not confuse what is convenient for power or tradition with what God says. Let us examine whether we are willing to hear his word even when it makes us uncomfortable, and whether we speak with courage and humility when God calls us to tell the truth.
exp.2:2:
It says that two people do not walk together unless they have agreed about where they are going. "Walk together" means going or traveling side by side, and having agreed means having come to a common decision about the destination.

The prophet Amos is speaking, sent by the LORD to Israel. God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt and that he knew them in a special way, which is why he will hold them accountable for their wrongdoing. The question opens a series of everyday examples: every effect has a cause. In this way, Amos explains that his message of judgment is not his own idea; God has sent him.

For today: if we want to walk with God, we need to agree with him about the way we should live, listen to his Word, and obey it. Closeness with God does not come from habit or from belonging to a people, but from a life aligned with his will.
exp.7:13:
This verse speaks of those who swear by "the guilt of Samaria," which refers to the false worship and idols of that city. They also swear by "your god, O Dan" and by "the way of Beersheba," rival places of worship. "Fall" means they will be brought down, and "never to rise again" announces a final judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, sent to the northern kingdom, Israel. Dan and Samaria were centers of false religion, and Beersheba in the south was also a place of popular worship. The people mixed their promises with idols. That is why God announces a famine of hearing his word, which comes just before this verse.

Today, we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. It is not enough to speak religious words if the heart rests on other things. Let us seek God sincerely while his word is within our reach.
exp.4:10:
The passage says that some in Israel mistreated the poor and took part of their grain through an unjust tax or some other form of abuse. To "trample" the poor means to crush them or humiliate them. The stones he mentions are large, finely cut blocks, a sign of costly houses. That is why God announces that these people will never live in the houses they built or drink the wine from the vineyards they planted.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom of Israel. Its leaders and the wealthy were oppressing the weak and rejecting anyone who corrected them at the gate, the place where judgment was given. God confronts them because injustice does not go unnoticed. The exact details of that taking of grain are not known with certainty.

For today: examine how you treat those who depend on you, such as employees or family members. Do not build your well-being on the abuse of others. Strive to pay what is fair, speak the truth, and listen to correction.
exp.2:12:
This verse is a call to pay attention. God commands the prophets to "hear" and to "testify," which here means to give a solemn witness or to warn with firmness, against the people of Israel, called "the house of Jacob." Moreover, God presents himself as "the Lord GOD, the God of Hosts," that is, the Lord with power over all.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier, he announced that an enemy would come and that only a small remnant would be saved. Now he asks that his warning be heard, because judgment is coming for the people's rebellion, injustice, and false security, even in their places of worship.

For today: When God warns us through his Word, we must not harden our hearts. Today you can read the Bible with humility, ask God to show you what you need to correct, and obey without delay.
exp.3:4:
Offer a thank offering of leavened bread, and loudly announce your freewill offerings. This is what you children of Israel love to do, declares the Lord GOD.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the northern kingdom, Israel. He speaks with sarcasm because they practiced their religion at Bethel and Gilgal, yet they lived in injustice and rebellion. Many understand that leavened bread was not in keeping with the law for certain offerings (Leviticus 2:11), although the thanksgiving offering did include loaves made with leaven (Leviticus 7:13). God was calling them to return to Him, not to show off.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our worship is sincere or only an appearance. God looks for a heart that repents and lives in justice, rather than religious acts that we want others to see.
exp.7:3:
He says that God calls the attention of those who "trample" the needy, that is, those who push down and use up the poor. "Do away with" means that they bring them to misery and ruin. "Hear" is a solemn command: listen to this.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, a man from the countryside sent to the kingdom of Israel. After the vision of the basket of ripe fruit, God announces that the end of the people is near. The accusations that follow show the reason: merchants who waited impatiently for the days of rest to end so they could keep selling, using short measures, inflated prices, and false scales.

Today it reminds us that God sees how we treat the weak in work and business. We can examine whether we pay what is fair, whether we keep what we promise, and whether we charge honestly, without taking advantage of those who are in need.
exp.8:10:
God promises that, on that future day, he will restore the house of David that has fallen. Here "tent" means a shelter, a symbol of David's royal family. "Gaps" are the breaks or openings in a wall. God says he will repair those gaps, restore what lies in ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. He has just announced judgment against Israel's sin, a sin that people believed would keep them safe. But not everything ends in punishment: God promises restoration. In Acts 15:16-17, James quotes this passage when speaking of how the Gentiles also seek the Lord. Christians see it fulfilled in Christ, a descendant of David; others also understand it as a promise for Israel's future.

For today: if you feel that your life or your family is in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild. Come to him with sincerity, and trust that his mercy has the last word.
exp.6:10:
This verse is part of what Amaziah tells the king. He reports that Amos said Jeroboam would die by the sword and that Israel would surely go into exile, away from their homeland. "By the sword" means through violence, that is, killed in battle. To go into exile means being forced to live in another country.

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, speaks here, accusing Amos before King Jeroboam II. Amos had announced judgment from God because of the people's injustice. However, Amaziah changes the message a little: Amos spoke about the house of Jeroboam, but he did not say in those words that the king himself would die. In this way Amaziah presents Amos as a traitor.

For today: sometimes the truth is uncomfortable, and people react by attacking the messenger. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his correction, and for courage to speak the truth with love.
exp.2:11:
The explanation says that, just as a shepherd rescues from a lion's mouth only two legs or a piece of an ear as proof that the sheep existed, so only a very small remnant of Israel will be saved. The words about having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch speak of a comfortable life; the end of the verse is understood in several ways, but the idea is that only remnants will remain.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa sent to the northern kingdom. Samaria was its capital, and its people lived in luxury while piling up wealth through injustice. God warns them that an enemy will destroy them, and that they will not be saved by their palaces or by their religion.

For today: let us not confuse comfort with security. Let us examine how we use what we have and whether we treat others with justice. Let us return to God before our losses force us to do so.
exp.8:6:
God asks the Israelites whether they are any more special to him than the Cushites, a distant people. He reminds them that he brought Israel up out of Egypt, but he also led the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir.

The Cushites were people from the land south of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who preached to the northern kingdom. The Israelites thought that being God's chosen people protected them from judgment, even though they lived in injustice. God shows them that he cares for all nations, and that their being chosen brings responsibility, not a privilege that allows sin. The exact locations of Caphtor and Kir are debated, but the meaning is clear.

Today, let us not assume that belonging to a believing church or family frees us from obeying God. He loves all peoples, and he calls us to live with humility and justice.
exp.3:12:
He is the Creator and owner of all things. He forms the mountains and creates the wind, that is, he made the mountains and the wind. "Reveals His thoughts to man" means that he shows people what they are thinking; nothing is hidden from him. "Turns the dawn to darkness" means that he turns darkness into dawn. "Strides on the heights of the earth" shows his rule over every place. His name is the LORD, the God of Hosts.

The prophet Amos speaks on God's behalf to the kingdom of Israel. God reminds them that he corrected them with many calamities, but they did not return to him. For this reason he calls them to prepare to meet their God. This verse shows them who it is they are dealing with: not a small god, but the Almighty.

Today, this verse invites us not to ignore God when he calls us. We can spend a few minutes praying sincerely, asking him to examine our thoughts and help us return to him.
exp.1:0:
This verse says God announces firm punishment against Moab. The phrase "For three transgressions, even four" is a way of speaking that means their wickedness has reached its limit. The words "I will not revoke My judgment" mean that God will not hold it back. The specific sin was that Moab burned the bones of Edom's king until they became lime, that is, white ash.

God speaks through the prophet Amos. Before speaking about Israel, God judges the neighboring nations. Desecrating the remains of a dead person was an act of hatred and contempt. The Bible does not say when this happened, so we do not know more details. It shows that God cares about justice even among peoples who are not his own.

For today: God sees even the offenses that no one else notices, and he cares about the dignity of every person, even that of an enemy. Today we can ask him for help not to return evil with contempt.
exp.7:8:
It says that God will do something very strange and frightening: the sun will go down in the middle of the day, and the earth will be left in darkness in the daytime. The phrase "in that day" simply points to a particular time that is coming. It is a picture of judgment, where what seemed most secure and clear suddenly turns dark.

God himself speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. The people lived with injustice, exploiting the poor, while they continued with their religious festivals. Some think the image recalls an eclipse, others that it is only figurative language about judgment. It cannot be said for certain which is the case.

For today: let us not confuse a comfortable or religious life with being right before God. Let us ask him to examine our hearts, and let us practice justice and compassion toward those around us, before the dark days arrive.
exp.3:7:
People stumbled from one town to the next looking for water, and they still went thirsty. The explanation points out that during a drought, people from two or three towns would walk to a single town that had water, yet it was never enough to satisfy them. To be satisfied means to be content and full. Even so, the people did not turn back to God.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. He reminds them that he sent hunger, drought, plagues, and death to get their attention. Many read this as the correction of a God who wanted to bring them back, not one who meant to destroy them. Each time, the passage ends with the same complaint: "you did not return to Me."

For today: when hardships keep coming back and nothing seems to satisfy us, it is worth asking whether God is inviting us to return to him. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but every difficulty can lead us to pray, examine our hearts, and draw near to God with humility.
exp.5:2:
They act as if the day of calamity were far off. The phrase "the day of calamity" refers to the time of God's judgment. Their dismissing that day, and bringing near a reign of violence, means that, without realizing it, they are bringing closer a rule built on violence and oppression. Some understand this to mean that they are preparing the seat of unjust power.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to Israel in a time of prosperity. He warns the comfortable leaders of Zion and Samaria who feel secure. They ignored the warnings and lived in luxury while injustice was present. The verses that follow show that life of feasting and music.

For today: do not put off repentance or settle into what God is pointing out to you. If you see an attitude or a pattern of unfair treatment in your life, correct it today, before the habit grows stronger.
exp.0:8:
God says he will punish Tyre, a city famous for its trade. The phrase "for three transgressions, even four" is a way of saying that its wickedness has reached its limit. The charge is that Tyre handed over a whole congregation of exiles to Edom, that is, it sold them as slaves. The covenant of brotherhood that it broke was a pact of friendship and mutual loyalty.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos, who announces judgment on several nations neighboring Israel. Tyre had made a friendship agreement with Israel (it is often linked to the alliance between Hiram and Solomon, though the text gives no further details). God judges cruelty and betrayal, even outside his own people.

Today: God pays attention to how we treat people, especially when promises are involved. Ask yourself whether there is some commitment or friendship you have neglected, and take a step to honor it.
exp.1:3:
God says that Judah sinned again and again, and because of this he will not hold back his judgment. The phrase "for three transgressions, even four" is a way of saying that their wickedness had reached its full measure. Judah rejected the Law of the Lord and did not keep his statutes. The "lies" are idols and false teachings, which led them astray, drawing them away from God, just as their fathers had walked.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. Earlier he judged neighboring nations; now the judgment reaches his own people. Judah knew the Law of God, so it bore greater responsibility. Afterward, the message is also directed to Israel.

For today: it is not enough to know the Word of God; it must be obeyed. Ask yourself what inherited or learned "lies" are pulling you away from God, and ask him to help you return to his truth with humility.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that the people of Israel carried a shrine and an idol that they had made for themselves. The BSB names them as Sakkuth, their king, and Kaiwan, their star god. The phrase "you have taken along" simply means "you carried." The "star god" seems to refer to a figure or symbol of a star-god. Scholars read and understand these names in different ways, so there is no single certain identification.

God speaks through the prophet Amos. He has just said that he wants true justice, not merely religious rituals. He reminds them that, even in the wilderness, their hearts were divided between him and other gods. For this reason he announces that they will be taken into exile, beyond Damascus.

For today: examine what things take the place of God in your heart, even when you faithfully attend church. Ask him to help you love him first and to live justly toward others.
exp.8:5:
It is he who builds his upper rooms in the heavens and founds his vault upon the earth; he who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth. The LORD is his name.

The verse says that God builds his dwelling in the heavens and sets his vault firmly upon the earth. The "upper rooms" are the chambers of a building high above, and the "vault" is the arching dome of the sky. It also says that God summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent to Israel with a message of judgment. Earlier it was said that no one would escape God, not even in captivity. This verse is like a hymn that explains why: the LORD who rules heaven, sea, and earth has no rival and no limits.

For today: when you feel that your problems or the world are out of control, remember who governs all things. This invites us to live with reverence and humility before God, and to trust that nothing escapes him.
exp.6:13:
Amos tells Amaziah that he is not a prophet, and he is not the son of a prophet, meaning he does not belong to any group or school of prophets. He was a herdsman, a man who tended livestock, and a tender of sycamore-fig trees, a humble job in the countryside. Some scholars also read Amos as saying "I am not a prophet by trade," since he did receive God's call.

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, ordered Amos to go away to Judah and stop speaking, because the king's sanctuary was there. Amos replies that he does not speak for a profession or for money, but because God himself took him from his work and sent him.

For today: God does not need impressive titles to use someone. If He calls you to speak the truth with love, be faithful where you are, even when others pressure you to be silent.
exp.5:7:
The Lord God has sworn by himself, and the Lord, the God of Hosts, declares that he detests the pride of Jacob. To detest something is to feel deep disgust toward it. He hates the citadels, meaning the strongholds of the wealthy, and so he will hand over the city and everything in it to the enemy.

The one speaking is God, and he speaks through the prophet Amos, who addressed the people of Israel. The wealthy lived in luxury, drank wine from large bowls, and did not grieve over the ruin of their people or over the poor. God does not condemn wealth in itself, but the pride and indifference that come with it.

Today we might ask ourselves: what do I trust in more, what I have or God? And also: does the suffering of others move me, or do I only care about my own comfort? Let us ask for a humble and compassionate heart.
exp.7:7:
God asks whether the land will not quake because of what has just been said, and whether all who live in it will not mourn. The land will swell up like the Nile when it floods its banks: "All of it will swell like the Nile" describes the rising; "it will surge" means it will be shaken; "and then subside" means it will sink back down again.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel. The verses before this accuse the rich of exploiting the poor, buying them for a trifling debt, and cheating in trade. God swears that he will not forget those deeds. The quaking is an image of his judgment. Some believe it refers to a real earthquake, and others take it as a figure of judgment.

For today: God sees how we treat the weak. Today you can examine whether you are just and honest in your work or your business, and help someone in need with concrete generosity.
exp.2:1:
He said God chose Israel in a special way among all the peoples. "Known" here does not mean only knowing who they are, but having a close relationship and choosing them. So "punish" means holding them to account for their wrongs. The "iniquities" are their sins and injustices. In short: because they were so close to God, Israel was more accountable.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Amos, a shepherd from Judah sent to the northern kingdom. God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt. Amos denounces social injustice and false religiosity. The verses that follow, with questions about the lion, show that this judgment has a cause and is not chance.

For today: being part of God's people is not a privilege to boast about, but an invitation to live with more sincerity and justice. We can ask God to show us in which areas we should change, and respond with humility.
exp.3:5:
God says he sent them "cleanness of teeth" in all their cities, meaning teeth left clean because there was nothing to chew, and "lack of bread" in all their towns. It was hunger. The verse says they did not return to God, and that they kept refusing to turn back to him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos to the kingdom of Israel. Earlier, with irony, he had told them to continue with their religion at Bethel and Gilgal, since their ceremonies were empty, without obedience or justice. The hunger was a warning to change course, but they did not respond.

For today: when lack or hardship comes, we can humbly ask whether God is calling us to return to him. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but it is always a good time to examine the heart and turn back to God.
exp.8:9:
It says that all the sinners among God's people will die by the sword. These are the ones who felt secure and said, "Disaster will never draw near or confront us." "By the sword" means by the sword, that is, in war. "Draw near" here means to come close to someone.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to Israel, the northern kingdom. They believed that, because they were the chosen people, they were safe, even though they lived in injustice. God announces judgment, but makes clear that he will not destroy Jacob completely: like grain that is shaken in a sieve, the sinners fall, but the good grain is preserved. Afterward he promises restoration.

For today: do not confuse God's grace with permission to live as you please. If you say, "Nothing will happen to me," examine your heart with humility, return to God, and trust in his mercy.
exp.4:18:
It says that the day of the LORD will be like a man who flees from a lion, only to encounter a bear. Then, thinking himself safe, he enters his house and rests his hand against the wall, and a snake bites him. "Encounter" means "come face to face with," and "rests" means "leans against." In other words, the danger does not end even in the place that seems safest.

The prophet Amos speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, Israel. Many people expected the day of the LORD as a day of victory and blessing. But Amos warns them that, because of their injustice and their empty religion, that day would be judgment and not light.

For today: it is not enough to practice a religion of appearances and feel secure. God desires a sincere heart that loves justice and mercy. Today you can ask him to examine your heart and correct what does not please him.
exp.2:0:
This verse opens a message from God. It calls the people to listen closely. The word "Hear" means "listen," and "the LORD" is the name of God. The message is directed "against you," that is, against you, the children of Israel. God reminds them that they are the family he brought up out of Egypt. The colon at the end signals that what follows is the message itself.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who ministered in the eighth century BC, during the time of the northern kingdom. God reminds them of their deliverance from Egypt because that rescue had placed them in a special relationship with him. That is why their disobedience was more serious. Some scholars think that "the whole family" also includes Judah, although the message is aimed mainly at the north.

For today: having received so much from God is no excuse for living carelessly, but a reason to obey him with greater care. Let us ask him for a heart ready to listen to his word.
exp.0:5:
God announces judgment against Gaza, a Philistine city. The phrase "For three transgressions... even four" is a way of speaking that shows the wrongdoing had piled up to the point where it could no longer be overlooked. "I will not revoke My judgment" means that God will not hold back the punishment. Gaza "exiled a whole population," that is, it took entire peoples away as prisoners and handed them over to Edom.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos, who also denounces other neighboring nations before speaking about Israel. God judges them for their cruelty and violence against other peoples. Many understand that this shows that God is just toward all nations, not only toward Israel. The exact historical details of this exile are not known with certainty.

For today: God sees how the weak are treated. Today we can ask ourselves whether in any way we take advantage of others, and ask him to make us just and compassionate people.
exp.8:12:
The explanation says that days are coming of such great abundance that the one plowing will overtake the one harvesting, and the one stomping grapes will overtake the one planting seed. The harvests will not end before the next one begins. "Sweet wine" is fresh grape juice, and "hills" are the low rises of land. Mountains dripping with sweet wine and hills flowing with it is an image of overflowing abundance.

God speaks through the prophet Amos. Earlier he announced judgment on Israel for its injustice, but he closes with hope: God will restore the fallen house of David and bring his people back to their land. Christians often see here a hope fulfilled in Christ, although there are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: even if you see ruins in your life or your family, God remains faithful and knows how to restore. Wait on Him with patience and keep working with confidence.
exp.4:3:
This passage says God speaks to the whole nation of Israel with a clear invitation: "Seek me and live!" The word "but" in this sentence marks a contrast with the sad news just before it. To "seek" God means to turn to him, to trust him, and to follow his way. "Live" speaks of a true life under his care, not merely of continuing to breathe.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos. Earlier he has announced that Israel will fall and be greatly reduced. Even so, God leaves a door open. The people were visiting religious places such as Bethel and Gilgal, but God asks them to seek him himself and not only their rituals.

For today: do not settle for religion out of habit. Set aside time to pray, read the Bible, and obey God. He still invites those who come to him with sincerity.
exp.4:13:
He says to seek what is good and not what is evil, so that you may truly live. "Seek" means to pursue with real effort. "Live" here speaks of a life that God blesses, not merely of breathing. The words "as you have claimed" show that the people said God was with them, and God tells them that this will be true only if they change the way they act.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the kingdom of Israel. The people believed God protected them, yet they oppressed the righteous, accepted bribes, and denied justice to the poor at the city gate, where legal disputes were settled.

For today: it is not enough to say "God is with me." That faith shows itself in concrete decisions. This week, choose to be just and honest in some small matter, such as your work or your dealings with others, even when no one sees you.
exp.1:5:
God says that Israel has sinned again and again, and for this reason he will not hold back its punishment. The saying "for three sins, and for four" is a way of speaking that shows the wickedness has reached its limit. Among their wrongs, they sold the righteous for money and the needy for a pair of sandals, that is, for something of very little value. The phrase "I will not revoke My judgment" means God will not cancel what he has decided.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos, who announces judgment on several nations. First he names Judah, and then he comes to Israel, the northern kingdom. The verses that follow show the problem: taking advantage of the poor, injustice, and false worship. Some think it refers to debts, but the text gives no further details.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat the weakest people with justice. For God, no person is worth less than a small profit.
exp.1:13:
It says that, when God's judgment comes, no one will be able to save themselves by their own abilities. Escape will fail the swift, the strong will not prevail by their strength, and the mighty will not save their lives.

Words in your verse that need a note: escape means having a way out; the swift are those who run quickly; and "prevail by his strength" means succeeding through all their power.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the kingdom of Israel. He accuses them of injustice and of refusing to listen: they made the Nazirites, who were dedicated to God, drink wine, and they silenced the prophets. For this reason he announces a punishment from which even the most capable will not be able to escape.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, talent, or resources as if they made us secure. It is wiser to listen to God with humility, correct what he points out, and seek his mercy before it is too late.
exp.5:0:
A warning of judgment, a "woe," is spoken against those who feel comfortable and secure in Zion, which is Jerusalem, and in Samaria, the capitals of Judah and Israel. To be at ease means to be comfortable and free of concern. Those who feel secure are the ones who rely on their own standing. They were the distinguished leaders of the foremost nation, and the house of Israel came to them for direction. Yet the verse says that the people of Israel will be brought down by an invasion, and their confidence will not save them.

The prophet Amos speaks here. He was a shepherd from Judah, sent by God to the northern kingdom, probably around the 8th century B.C. The leaders lived in luxury and ignored injustice and danger. God confronts them because their comfort hid pride and a lack of obedience.

For today: examine whether your peace comes from trusting God or from having everything under control. Ask Him to wake you up to live with humility, justice, and compassion.
exp.5:9:
This verse describes a very sad scene after a terrible punishment. A close relative comes to the house to pick up the bodies and burn them. He calls out to someone hiding inside and asks whether anyone else is still with them. The answer is "None." Then the relative tells them to be silent, because the name of the LORD must not be spoken. Some believe they feared attracting more judgment; others think they no longer wanted to call on God. The text does not make this clear.

God speaks through the prophet Amos to the kingdom of Israel, which was living in luxury, pride, and injustice. He warns them that their false sense of security will end in judgment.

Today, this passage invites us not to take God lightly while we live at ease. It is better to turn back to him in time and seek justice, rather than falling silent about his name when hardship arrives.
exp.7:9:
God says he will turn the feasts of Israel into weeping, and their joyful songs into songs of grief. Songs of grief are sad songs sung for the dead. Sackcloth was rough clothing worn as a sign of sorrow, and shaving the head was also done to show mourning. The sorrow will be like that of parents who lose their only son, and the end will be like a bitter day.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. They had festivals and religious life, but they oppressed the poor and sought unjust gain (Amos 8:4-6). For this reason the Lord announces judgment: what they now celebrate will become sorrow.

For today: it is not enough to sing and attend gatherings if we live with injustice. Ask God whether there is something in how you treat others, in your work, or with your money that you should correct. Repenting in time is better than weeping afterward.
exp.6:5:
It says that the LORD relented, that is, he changed his plan and decided not to send the judgment of fire he had shown Amos. "It will not happen either" means that this destruction would not take place. "Either" recalls that he had already called off another vision, the one of the locusts.

The narrator is the prophet Amos, who tells of God's response. Amos had interceded: "O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech you: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." Israel was in sin, but the prophet asked for mercy. God listened. Even so, the next vision, the one of the plumb line, shows that his patience had a limit. Scholars understand the idea of God relenting in several ways, but they all agree that it shows his compassion.

For today: pray for others, for your family, your church, or your country, with humility and confidence that God is merciful. Do not use his patience as an excuse to keep living the same way; use it as an opportunity to return to him.
exp.3:8:
God says he struck Israel with blight and mildew that ruined their growing gardens and vineyards, and the locust devoured their fig and olive trees. Fig orchards are fields planted with fig trees. Despite all this, the people did not come back to God. Returning means turning back to God, turning away from wrongdoing and repenting.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, in the middle of the eighth century B.C., to the northern kingdom, Israel. They were a people who were prosperous in religion and in material things, but unjust toward the poor. These losses were meant as a call for them to respond and return to him. The same refrain is repeated: "yet you did not return to Me."

Today: when difficulties come, ask God whether he wants to speak to you. Do not harden your heart; return to him with humility and sincerity.
exp.4:9:
They hated the one who corrected them in the gate, and they despised the one who spoke with integrity. The "gate" was the entrance of the city, where the elders and judges handled cases and settled disputes. Someone who "reproves" calls attention to wrongdoing. To "despise" someone means to look down on them and reject what they say.

God speaks through the prophet Amos, who was sent to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people were committing injustices: they oppressed the poor and accepted bribes in judgment. When someone in the court denounced this, they rejected that person. God, whom Amos presents as Creator and Lord of all, does not overlook that injustice.

For today: when someone corrects us with truth and good intention, let us not react with anger. Let us listen with humility and ask ourselves whether God is speaking to us through that person.
exp.0:13:
God himself says he will set fire to the walls of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. The fire will consume its citadels amid war cries on the day of battle, like a violent wind on a day of storm. The verse itself describes the scene, and the image is of swift destruction that cannot be stopped.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Amos. The Ammonites were neighbors of Israel, and they had committed a terrible cruelty: they ripped open pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge their territory. God does not overlook violence against the innocent, even when it is committed by another nation. The following verse announces that their king will go into exile.

For today: God sees injustice and has compassion on the weak. We must not seek our own gain at the expense of others, and we can trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.6:11:
Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, tells Amos to leave. He calls him "seer," which was another word for prophet, and here it sounds like contempt. He tells him to go away to the land of Judah, to earn his bread there and to do his prophesying there, but not in Bethel.

Amaziah served in the sanctuary of King Jeroboam, in the northern kingdom. Amos, who came from Judah, had announced judgment against Israel. Amaziah had accused him before the king, and now he tries to get him out of the place. The message bothers him, so he wants to silence the messenger. Some think he is hinting that Amos prophesied for money, although the text does not say this clearly.

Today, we sometimes prefer to silence what makes us uncomfortable rather than examine it. Before rejecting a correction, it is wise to ask ourselves humbly before God: what if this is true, and I need to hear it?
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces the prophet Amos and the time when he received his message. It says he was "among the sheepherders of Tekoa," meaning a man who looked after flocks, not a professional prophet. The verse says what he "saw" concerning Israel, which means God gave him a vision or message about the nation. The kings named are Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam, son of Jehoash, of Israel.

Amos speaks in the 8th century B.C., when both kingdoms were enjoying times of prosperity. An earthquake is mentioned, which other biblical texts also recall, but we do not know exactly when it happened. The message comes from God, and Amos only passes it on.

For today: God can speak and use ordinary, humble people. You do not need an important position to be faithful; it is enough to listen to God and obey him in your place of work and in your life.
exp.5:4:
They sing and improvise songs to the sound of the harp. They also invent musical instruments of their own, thinking of themselves as being like David, the famous singer and songwriter of Israel.

The prophet Amos speaks for God to the comfortable and wealthy leaders of Israel and Judah. They lived in luxury, with banquets and music, while ignoring the injustice and suffering of their people, here called "Joseph." Therefore God announces that they will be among the first to go into exile. Some understand that he is mocking them, since they copied David's art but without his heart of worship.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I use my gifts and my free time only for my own comfort? Let us ask God for a heart that is sensitive to the pain of others and willing to help.

sum.6: God showed Amos a plague of locusts and a judgment by fire, but Amos pleaded for Israel, and God relented. Then God showed him a plumb line: God would measure his people, and would no longer overlook their sin. Amaziah tried to silence Amos, but Amos replied that God had called him, and he announced judgment against Amaziah.
sum.3: God rebukes the wealthy women of Samaria who oppress the poor, and announces that they will be taken away as captives. He reminds them that he sent famine, drought, plagues, and destruction, yet they never returned to him. Therefore they must prepare to meet God, the Creator of all things.
sum.2: God reminds the Israelites that he chose them and brought them out of Egypt, and for that reason he will hold them accountable for their wickedness. Using simple questions, he explains that nothing happens without a cause and that he warns people through his prophets. Samaria, full of oppression and robbery, will be torn down, and its palaces and altars will be destroyed.
sum.7: God shows Amos a basket of ripe fruit and announces that the end has come for Israel, because of the injustice of those who cheat and exploit the poor. There will be judgment, mourning, and darkness. A famine will come, not of bread or water, but of hearing the word of God, and people will search for it and not find it. Those who swear oaths by idols will also fall.
sum.5: God warns the leaders of Israel who live at ease, in luxury, and in false security, without grieving over the ruin of their people. Because of their pride and their injustice, which turns justice into bitterness, God will send an enemy nation that will destroy their houses and lead them into exile, at the head of those carried away.
sum.8: God announces that no one will be able to escape his judgment, whether by hiding on the highest mountains, in the deepest places, or in exile, because Israel sinned and believed it was safe. Even so, he will not destroy it completely. He promises to raise up the fallen tent of David, restore his people, give them back their abundance, and plant them forever in their land.
sum.0: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, announces that God speaks with a voice like thunder from Jerusalem. God declares judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon for their cruelty, for handing over captives, and for betraying their brothers. This teaches that God sees violence and injustice, and does not overlook them.
sum.4: Amos laments that Israel has fallen and calls the people to seek God and live, not to the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal. He denounces those who oppress the poor and pervert justice at the city gate, and warns that the day of the LORD will be darkness for them. God rejects their festivals and songs, and asks that justice roll down like a mighty stream.
sum.1: God announces punishment on Moab, Judah, and Israel for their sins. He accuses Israel of mistreating the poor and despising the prophets, even though God had brought them out of Egypt and given them the land. For this reason, neither the strong nor the swift will be able to escape.
